inline.s: The abbot of Fayun Monastery, Miaorong, whose personal name was Guangcheng, and the abbot of Qixia Monastery, Jianru, whose personal name was Ciren, had both been among the dharma-attendants who, on the days when the shrine was welcomed and sent forth, twice traveled back and forth to Caoxi. They told in full how our teacher, in the winter of the renxu year, on the eleventh day of the eleventh month, because the provincial treasurer Wu Shengbo, the Shaozhou governor Zhang Sanxing, and his Guangdong disciple, the licentiate Liu Qixiang, had time and again sent letters to Wuru earnestly inviting him, and had even sent the hall-master of Baolin, Ben’ang, to come and receive him--our teacher then resolved to leave Mount Kuang and enter Caoxi. On that very day he ascended the seat in the Wuru dharma-hall and made it known to hall-master Ang, and likewise took leave of the assembly. He sat cross-legged for a long while, unaware that a great serpent had coiled itself beneath his body, its form pressed flat as a cushion. When he rose and saw it, he took it as an omen and lit a flame to accompany the journey; it also prefigured that, having entered Caoxi, he would remain but a single year and never return to Wuru again. On the day he arrived back at Caoxi, hall-master Ang invited him to ascend the hall and preach. Word by word he broke open the old case of the Sixth Patriarch’s bodily relic and the incense-offerings, and the meaning of how what came before and what came after answer each other; therein one sees the spirit of one who knows beforehand. The dharma-words ran: “Before the Sixth Patriarch came forth into the world, he was only a wood-seller of Xinzhou. Because he had planted the spiritual root in former lives and long nourished his practice, the instant he heard the Diamond Sutra spoken and the line ‘should dwell nowhere,’ he cut off the birth-and-death of eons, awakened to his own mind, and so received the robe and bowl of Huangmei. Is not the Baolin of today come down from the shoulder that bore the firewood and the waist-stone that husked rice? Hence it has such vast and boundless brightness that fills the whole world. Every word, every phrase of the Chan school flows from that firewood-shoulder and that husking waist-stone, and so today the incense and offerings are no different from when he was alive. The flesh-body, firm and unrotting, is no different from one who speaks the Dharma now. Such blessings too come from that firewood-shoulder and that husking waist-stone. This beam of prajñā-light that the Sixth Patriarch awakened to, every person has a share of, lacking not a hair’s breadth. If one can but awaken to one’s own mind, then one may churn the long river into ghee and turn the vast earth into gold; plucking up a single blade of grass, make it a sixteen-foot golden body; and with that sixteen-foot golden body, serve as a single blade of grass. Naturally one then possesses great spiritual powers, transforming freely at will, doing whatever one pleases, nothing impossible.” He further said: “Our teacher, re-entering Caoxi, had it in mind to rebuild the great hall of Caoxi. The many monies he had raised from the three offices and the prefectures went entirely to purchasing iron-pyrus timber in western Guangdong and, as recorded in the chronicle under the wushen year, had already been hauled into Caoxi. The two gentlemen Wu and Zhang, together with hall-master Ang, shared in this vow, and so their pleas for his return were all the more devout. And our teacher, knowing that his hour had come, said, ‘When conditions and the times run contrary, where shall the transformation find a place to lodge?’ And so, in the winter of the guihai year, upon the thirteenth day of the tenth month, he passed away.” There was, moreover, a plot that the vice-minister Xiao Xuanpu had asked the governor Zhang to divine for a shadow-hall, two li south of Nanhua Monastery in Shaozhou, named Tianzi Gang, the Hill of the Son of Heaven. An old prophecy said: “Head above Tianzi Hill, feet treading the Yellow Mud Pond; whoever is buried here, from generation to generation a Dharma-king will arise.” The Guangdong congregation, having taken refuge, therefore raised a stūpa on that spot and there interred his whole body. The Wuru disciple Fushan, styled Zhiwei, together with Shenshen, styled Yihui, Guangyi, styled Xuzhong, and Ciren, styled Jianru, hastened to Guangdong to receive the shrine but could not gain it. So they went about in the Wu-Yue region and, by the teacher’s last command, laid the matter before the many patrons: Wu Benru, He Zhiyue, Wang Jie’an, and Qian Shouzhi. These wrote to the Guangdong judicial commissioner Lu Jingye, who sent a dispatch to Shaozhou; and on the twenty-first day of the first month of the yichou year the shrine was opened and borne back to Mount Kuang. As the land there was dank and damp, Fushan built a stūpa-court and set the shrine floating upon it. The prefectural judge of Nankang, Qian Woxin, whose personal name was Qizhong, chose a place and buried it. Eleven years later, in the yihai year, fierce tigers rose up in the mountains, and Fayun could no longer keep his congregation at peace. Fushan blamed the unquiet spot of the stūpa, and again brought the shrine forth to its floating platform, where he saw that the protecting enclosure had been half eaten by ants, and he dared not divine a tomb. Nine more years passed, and in the ninth month of the guiwei year the Lingnan disciple, the minister Chen Zizhuang, sent a letter with plenty of provisions to greet it. It happened that the Guangdong disciple Liu Qixiang, serving in the penal office of Ruizhou, was auditing the stores of Nankang, and he threw himself into the task of returning the shrine to Caoxi. When they reached Meiling, there was the newly appointed commander-in-chief of Guangdong, Song Zhaoming, named Ji, who ten years earlier, beneath the banner of the Guangdong governor-general, had formed a dharma-affinity with our teacher. Crossing the ridge to take up office, he chanced upon the spiritual shrine and, marveling beyond measure at his fortune, ordered his soldiers to shoulder the shrine and personally escorted it into Caoxi. Months after taking his post he came again to Caoxi, where the shrine-bearing disciples Guangcheng, styled Miaorong, and Cili, styled Jianchi, seeing a crack in the shrine, secretly bored a small opening through it to peep within, and there beheld the master seated upright as though alive. They were debating whether to open the shrine, but no one dared decide. When Song heard this, he at once drew his blade and split the crack open, and they saw the twin cross-legged feet as if alive, the nails and hair both grown long and of a bright red. The robe and shoes were still new, and only when they met the wind did they crumble and fall to pieces, laying bare the five limbs. Suddenly a monk arrived and asked that, following the Indian rite, powdered sandalwood from Hainan be smeared over the body until it was like lacquer; the smearing done, he departed. Long before, in Caoxi, an unmarried girl had vowed to embroider a robe of a thousand Buddhas to offer in homage; fearing that her breath was unclean, she wrapped her mouth in yellow silk as she plied the needle and thread. When the robe was finished, our teacher had already passed on into the shrine, and the robe was left in a chest of the Baolin storehouse. One day the abbot-monk, celebrating a penitential rite, wished to don this robe, but the monks clamored and stopped him. Later, when our teacher’s flesh-body returned to Caoxi and came forth from the shrine, the purple gauze robe was suddenly blown to shreds by the wind, and the countryfolk snatched up the pieces as auspicious tokens. So they took the thousand-Buddha robe the girl had embroidered and clothed him in it; the robe had lain in the chest twenty-two years, yet its luster was as fresh as new. Thereupon it was enshrined at the site of the old stūpa-court, and the monastery was named Hanshan, half a li from the Baolin hall of Nanhua Monastery. The disciples attended him after the manner in which the Sixth Patriarch is attended at Baolin: at dawn they bring a basin of hot fragrant water, steam his face until it sweats, wipe it with a cloth, and set before him food and drink with full reverent offerings, exactly as though he were alive. Once a year they bathe him, and the water of the washing is taken by the countryfolk to drink for the healing of sickness, and it is gone in a moment. Every year the pilgrims of Caoxi, in the second and the eighth months, all the people of the province entering the mountains to pay their respects, would, after offering incense to the Sixth Patriarch, proclaim that they had come to offer incense to the Seventh Patriarch; and so the title “the Seventh Patriarch of Caoxi” arose. For the Guangdong pilgrims, of one accord, had in mind that bodhisattva in flesh, and in a single moment from the Southern Sea to the Northern Sea, all within the realm heard this name and took it as a matter of course. Yet certain critics held that one must not overstep the five lineages and schools, nor yield to a passing word-of-mouth transmission, for fear of giving a handle to those who would later revise the lamp-lineage as a single orthodox succession. Zhen, not measuring his own worth, hastily composed three treatises--on the dharma of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, on the robe and bowl, and on the flesh-body--to lay before the clear-eyed.

Zhen remarks: Above Śākyamuni are called the seven Buddhas; from Śākyamuni’s transmission to Kāśyapa and below, on to Bodhidharma, they are called the twenty-eight patriarchs of the West. From Bodhidharma’s crossing east and below, on to Caoxi, they are called the six patriarchs of the East; they are not called Buddhas, nor are they simply called masters. The Sixth Patriarch transmitted to Huairang and to Xingsi alone, two branches only. Huairang dwelt on Mount Heng, and so his line is called the Nanyue line, and he transmitted to Mazu. Nanyue is not recorded as being called a patriarch, yet Mazu is uniquely honored as patriarch. Is this not to say that Mazu gave the dharma to the many, and did not receive it as a single transmitter of the robe and bowl? Under Mazu came Baizhang, and under Baizhang came Huangbo; these are called great masters or Chan masters, and are never heard called lineage-tutors, for at that time there was yet no teaching of a division into schools. Under Huangbo came Linji, and it is here that the Linji school is first named; the title of a school begins from that time. Before this there were the names of two branches, but no gates of two schools. Under Baizhang there was also Guishan, and under Guishan came Yangshan; and so arose the Guiyang school. Thus one branch of Baizhang gave rise to two schools. Xingsi dwelt at Qingyuan, and so his line is called the Qingyuan line, transmitting to Shitou; under Shitou came Dongshan, and under Dongshan came Caoshan, and by the easy slip of the tongue they were confusedly called the Caodong school. Under Shitou there was also Xuefeng, and under Xuefeng came Yunmen, called the Yunmen school. Later there was also the Fayan school. Thus one branch of Qingyuan gave rise to three schools. Now Huairang and Qingyuan are of one generation, Mazu and Shitou of the next, Baizhang and Xuefeng of yet another--three generations below the Sixth Patriarch--and in none of these do we hear the name of a school. Even Huangbo, of the fourth generation, is not heard to stand with Guishan, Dongshan, and Yunmen of the same generation to contend over the name of a school. This is precisely why Huangbo towers above his fellows and dared to take Mazu to task. Huangbo once said, “Within the great Tang there is no Chan master.” A monk asked, “The venerable ones of all quarters gather the assembly and open the teaching; why then do you say there is no Chan master?” Huangbo said, “I do not say there is no Chan; I say only that there is no master. Do you not see that beneath Master Ma there were eighty-four who sat in the dharma-court, and of those who obtained Master Ma’s true dharma-eye there were only two or three, and among them was the monk Guizong? A man who has left the home-life must know the matter that has been transmitted from above. Thus, even one of the fourth patriarch’s heirs like Niutou, who spoke at length and in breadth, still did not know the pivotal device that points upward. With this eye one can distinguish the true from the false in the schools. But when it touches one’s own present affairs one cannot grasp it; one only knows to recite phrases, to stuff them into the skin-bag, and to go about saying ‘I understand Chan.’ Can that take the place of your birth-and-death? To make light of the elder masters is to fall into hell as swiftly as an arrow flies.” Great indeed are the words of Huangbo! The wisdom-eye and the dharma-eye truly do not deceive me; only the direct grandson of Mazu could carry on so. This is what is meant by “blue comes from indigo yet is deeper than indigo,” and “curdle comes from milk yet is finer than milk.” When Linji made the division into schools, Huangbo gained many sons; and Guiyang, Caodong, Yunmen, and Fayan, following one after another in fame, split the gates and divided the households, and so Mazu, Baizhang, Shitou, and Xuefeng gained many grandsons. One flower and five leaves: we never hear of the flower and the leaves being marked as the root and the trunk. Only because root and trunk are not two does the fruit ripen whole. If one flower can become a hundred, a thousand, ten thousand million flowers, and five leaves can become fifty, a hundred, a thousand, ten thousand million leaves, then the more flowers the more leaves; and as the saying goes, “When the leaves are many the flower does not bloom; when the flowers are many the fruit does not set.” Though the words be small, they can illustrate something great. If everyone chases flowers and pursues leaves, where shall one ask after the root and the trunk? Even if fruit can be had, it is only fruit grafted from a flower onto a strange stock; where does the root lie? I am so foolish as not to understand wherein the reality of the schools truly consists. “The ten thousand dharmas return to the One”--this is the teaching. “Where does the One return?”--this is the school. The dharma abides in the hearts of all under heaven, and the heart of the dharma cannot have five. The school abides in the heart of a good and wise teacher; how then should the heart of the school have five? When Bodhidharma came west, those who knew him called it only the Chan school; if the school has five, then the mind has five and Chan has five. I am too dull to see wherein the reality of the five schools truly lies. The five schools are gates; they are titles. The gate of a patriarch is in no wise different from the gate of a Buddha; the title of a patriarch is finally no different from the title of a Buddha. He who can become a patriarch must be able to become a Buddha, and he who cannot become a Buddha must surely not be able to become a patriarch. A patriarch comes from the Buddhas and the bodhisattvas. To give him another title, that is permissible; to give him another gate, I fear it is not. Still more, to take five titles and set up five gates is like the children and grandchildren of a household seizing upon the ancestral estate and scattering the family goods in disorder; this I do not understand. As to the division of titles, it is not only the Buddhas and patriarchs that are divided. Even Śākyamuni has ten titles, and the Buddhas and bodhisattvas have countless and boundless titles; these cannot be held up as equal. As to the union of gates, it is not only the Buddhas and patriarchs that unite. Even the Tiantai dharmanature school, which follows the Lotus and Nāgārjuna’s Madhyamaka; the Xianshou school, which follows the Avataṃsaka and the contemplation of the dharma-realm; the Nanshan Vinaya school; the Cīen Dharmalakṣaṇa school, which illumines the Consciousness-only school; and the Vajraśekhara Yoga three-mystery school--every teaching must have a school; without a school no teaching is established. They cannot be split into two. If they may be divided and made two, they must surely belong to the heretics, the outer paths, and the Lesser Vehicle. Know that the Pure Land is the mind alone; this is the ten thousand dharmas returning to the One. The patriarch can come west; the Buddha can return west. From the west and from the east, from the south and from the north, none who think but submit--this is what is meant by Buddha and Patriarch. The Dharma of the Buddha is equal, with no high and low. That titles differ, how can one hold them to be equal? Yet for rebirth and for the upholding of the Dharma, one must first have the title. The flesh-eye takes refuge wholly in the reverent name. Long ago I saw a Chan worthy whom the vulgar called “Lord”; Yunqi forbade it and it ceased. This is the meaning of Confucius’s rectification of names and the Spring and Autumn’s fixing of ranks. In the present worldly order, unless one has founded a state and carried on a house, one may not be called a patriarch; yet among the hundred crafts and the myriad trades, all may be called master. In the world-transcending order, they are called the twenty-eight patriarchs of the West and the six patriarchs of the East, and are not heard to be called mere masters. Mazu obtained the dharma from Caoxi and Nanyue before the schools were divided; therefore it is fitting to call him patriarch. Hanshan too obtained the dharma from Caoxi, and going to and fro between Nanyue and Qingyuan, in every place, in every moment, did nothing but speak the dharma, practice the dharma, and transmit the dharma. Though he came after the schools were divided, he still returns to the time before they were divided; therefore it is fitting, following the precedent of Mazu, to call him Patriarch Hanshan. Only those who personally attended him may call him our teacher; those who inherit the dharma may call him the master of the house. As for the titles of great master and seventh patriarch, these all go along with the common custom. The Jingzong Record quotes the words of Bodhidharma: “To illumine the mind-school of the Buddha, with no error whatsoever, and to have practice and understanding answer each other--this is called a patriarch.” These words match perfectly the meaning of “Patriarch Hanshan.” If the great master Daguan, in his verse in praise of Master Hanshan that he sent with the image of Master Kang, says that the flesh-Buddha of Caoxi has appeared, he means Patriarch Lu. Patriarch Lu may be called the flesh-Buddha, and Patriarch Hanshan should be no different; so let us call him the flesh-Patriarch of Caoxi. The Chan monks who push themselves forward in the world can truly bear no comparison. In general, only the schools, the dharma, and the vinaya may be called lineage-tutors, dharma-masters, and vinaya-masters; one may not call them lineage-patrims, dharma-patrims, and vinaya-patrims. Only when the three gates are hard to name might one be called patriarch. Thus Patriarch Lu,’ obtaining the school from Huangmei, the dharma from Yinzong, and the vinaya from Zhiguang, is a model for Mazu, for Hanshan, and for those who come again in later ages.

Zhen further notes, in the outline of the life of Patriarch Lu: When the patriarch had received the robe and the dharma from Huangmei, he came to the South Sea and met the dharma-master Yinzong, who, hearing the words about the wind and the banner, invited the patriarch into his room, held the ritual of a disciple, and announced to the four assemblies, “This Layman Lu is a bodhisattva in the flesh.” Gathering the famous worthies, he shaved his head; and further, before the vinaya-master Zhiguang of the Fahsing Monastery, he received the full precepts. That ordination platform had been set up by the Tripitaka master Guṇabhadra in the time of the Liu Song. That master had recorded, “Hereafter a bodhisattva in the flesh shall receive the precepts on this platform.” From this we know that the patriarch who confers the robe and the bodhisattva in the flesh must be one person, while the monk who shaves the head, the master who confers the precepts, and the tutor who confers the dharma must not be one person. This mind is the same, this way is the same, but their meaning is distinct and their rule is distinct. Again, Patriarch Lu said to the four assemblies, “I have unworthily received the robe and the dharma of Master Ren; now I preach the dharma for you, but I do not transmit the robe.” And one day he said to his disciples, “I wish to return to Xinzhou.” The great assembly, mourning, begged the patriarch to remain and said, “Master, when you go from here, will you come back sooner or later?” The patriarch said, “The leaf falls and returns to the root; when I come, I shall have no mouth.” Again they asked, “From whom did the master’s dharma-eye descend?” The patriarch said, “The one who has the Way obtains it; the one who is without a mind penetrates it.” From this we know that the robe and bowl of the patriarchs had long been without vestige since the Xiantian years of the early Tang. As for the robe and bowl now handed down at Caoxi, they did not come from Huangmei but were bestowed in the Shenlong first year of Emperor Zhongzong of Tang, who dispatched the eunuch Xue Jian to invite him; Patriarch Lu, declining on the grounds of illness, did not go, and thus discoursed with Xue Jian, saying that the Way is realized by the mind, and not by sitting in meditation and practicing concentration. His words were very full. Xue Jian, receiving the instruction, was suddenly enlightened, took his leave and returned to court, and memorialized the patriarch’s words. An edict thanked the master and bestowed upon him a kṣāya of worn patches, five hundred bolts of silk, and one bowl. From this we know that the robe and bowl of Caoxi are only the royal offerings, not the token of the Fifth Patriarch. It is Mazu alone who transmitted the dharma the most, and even his disciples had many disagreements; therefore one may speak of his transmission of the dharma, but not of his transmission of the robe and bowl, nor of a transmission of a token, nor of a transmission of a school. To take a material thing as a token of transmission is something the outer paths often have. How could Mazu have so many robes and bowls? The story about the robe and bowl that is handed down is, through a thousand years, mere dust for food and mud for soup; the life of the Buddhas and patriarchs is in no way bound up with it. Only our Hanshan, a patriarch in the flesh, inherits the transmission of one flower and five leaves, so as to reach a hundred, a thousand, ten thousand, a hundred million leaves. Set against those who raise a stick or give a shout, who point directly and transmit in a single line, one does not know which is the word that fits the head. “The one who has the Way obtains it; the one who is without a mind penetrates it”--the karmic meeting of Patriarch Lu gains all the more belief today. Truly, the former sage and the later sage accord in the one standard.

Zhen again read the Sevenfold Revision of Lang Gongying and found: When the Sixth Patriarch passed away, the officials and disciples of Guangzhou, Shaozhou, and Xinzhou all strove to receive the true body, and the assembly could not decide. So they burned incense and prayed, saying, “Wherever the incense points, there shall the master return.” Because the incense pointed to Caoxi, they moved the shrine together with the robe and bowl, built a stūpa, and enshrined him. Then the flesh-body came forth from the stūpa-shrine, the incense having perfumed it like lacquer; when one stroked the beard and hair by hand, they were as though three or four days after a shaving. During the rebellion of Huang Chao, the brigands came to Caoxi and would have desecrated it, but a wind and murk darkened the daylight, and they bowed in reverence, begged for mercy, and went away. At the end of the Song, in the poem of Prime Minister Wen Tianxiang on looking toward Nanhua Monastery, are the lines: “On and on I come to Nanhua, as if hurried through a dream; the Buddha’s transformation, how much dust of knowing, and the sorrow is the same as mine.” The gentleman’s own note says that the Sixth Patriarch’s flesh-body was wounded by the rebel troops; but this is merely a means by which he lodged his own self-consolation in the poem. The title speaks of “looking toward” Nanhua, so he had never himself seen it. The Gazetteer of Caoxi, which Hanshan himself compiled, records: In the second year of Xiantian of Emperor Zhongzong of Tang, the master passed into nirvāṇa at Guoen Monastery in Xinzhou, and his whole body was placed in the Caoxi stūpa. In the tenth year of Kaiyuan of Emperor Xuanzong, a filial son Zhang Man, having received twenty strings of cash from the Silla monk Jin Dabei, was hired to take the patriarch’s head back to the sea-east for offering. The county magistrate Yang Kan and the prefect Liu Wutian, obtaining the writ, captured the thief and examined his case, and only because the patriarch’s disciple Lingtao pleaded with all his might was his life spared. Thereupon they moved the true body to the Faith-and-Vessel Tower so that it might be guarded, and the tower was later changed into the Patriarchs’ Hall. At the beginning of the Kaibao era of Emperor Taizu of Song, when the imperial army pacified the South Sea, the remnant troops of the Liu family made trouble, and the patriarch’s stūpa and hall were reduced to ashes. The true body, protected by the stūpa-keeping monk, suffered not the slightest loss. In the tenth year of Tiansheng of Emperor Renzong, a peaceful carriage was made ready and the patriarch’s true body, together with the robe and bowl, was received into the palace and offered to, and thereafter a messenger was sent with an edict to return them to Caoxi. In Hanshan’s Gazetteer of Caoxi there is a hymn in praise of the Sixth Patriarch’s flesh-body: “When the one yang returns, the warm air gradually comes. The three yangs fulfilled, all things are in spring. When the one yin first arrives, the flowing fire congeals within. When the three yins begin to join, the grass and trees are suddenly withered. The powerful maker of change still causes withering and flourishing; how much more so does the unborn, in thought after thought, in fragrance after fragrance, entering the void from what is, the four elements all dissolving; entering what is from the void, what is then is undecaying. When the void and what is are both forgotten, it is the same as the diamond. The mountains, rivers, and the great earth are all the everlasting still-light. Therefore our master is the king of the dharma.” Zhen, having fully examined the records of the gazetteer, knows that the flesh-body of Patriarch Lu was never in any way wounded. The stūpa and the true body now both abide in the monastery, though not in the same place. Compared with Hanshan, after his passing and the many years, the going in and out of the stūpa-shrine, the former patriarch and the later patriarch are as if from a single track. The sutra says that for one who is greatly enlightened, the dharma-body and the reward-body are in no way two, and that he who does not treasure the reward-body is an outer-path heretic. Nāgārjuna says that a bodhisattva newly on the ground, whose Way is not yet full, may indeed have the affair of burning the body. And the sutra says that a bodhisattva who never retreats has not the eighty myriad worms in the body, and therefore the flesh-body does not decay, the hair and the nails can grow, the dignity gathers beings, and through eons the fragrant light endures. Even as the First Patriarch returned to the west, and the Second Patriarch Shenguang, and the Fourth and Fifth Patriarchs of Huangmei, all had flesh-bodies, so we know the flesh-body is to be treasured and cannot be compared with burning the body. To regard it as a flesh-body is thus; to regard it as the dharma-body is also thus. To regard it with the flesh-eye is thus; to regard it with the dharma-eye is also thus.

One asked, saying: You have spoken at length that the teaching and the school return to the One, and the principle that all things return to the Pure Land, even down to the matter of the Caoxi Sixth Patriarch’s robe, bowl, and flesh-body, so that the long night is made to dawn, the heavy mist to see the sun; it is indeed trustworthy and perfect, with no meaning left out, and the heart’s regard for Patriarch Hanshan has no regret either. The sincere man completes himself and completes things; the gentleman acts first and speaks afterward. But as for you yourself, at the juncture of birth and death, of going and coming, how do you place yourself? He answered: As for my own placing of myself, it is not only the teaching, the school, and the Pure Land that return to the One; even the teachings of Confucianism, of Buddhism, of Daoism, and the ten thousand dharmas none of them fail to return to the One. Nor is it only in the chronicle of my teacher Hanshan, in the concluding discourse at the end, that the Way is spoken of as One. From the two classics of Confucius and Mencius, through the eight thousand scrolls of the Seen-Sages’ Compendium, the two thousand scrolls collected amid the new poems, down to the two classics of the Nanhua and the Lisao held up for a second glance, the Immortal Ancestor Jingsheng’s Book of Transformation, and the Dao-scriptures, whatever has been set down by the pen, nothing fails to be of the principle of “one Way amid the three teachings.” And yet words must have their root; the truthful message may be verified again. I quote the scriptures and cite the traditions, I bring the ancients to prove the present, and I presume to say that I transmit and do not compose, that I do not fabricate what I have not learned. The heart’s regard for my teacher Hanshan is not a turning from Confucius to the Buddha, nor a turning from the Immortal Ancestor to the patriarch. Whatever my teacher trod in his person, whatever he spoke from his mouth, whatever he wrote with his brush, all were of the principle of “one Way amid the three teachings,” without need of the kind of riving that the good and wise layman Fu Dashi, amid his very speaking and moving in robe and cap, set forth face to face for Emperor Wu of Liang. For example, among his writings beyond the Buddhist canon are An Explanation of the Analects, A Direct Pointer to the Doctrine of the Mean, Resolving Doubts on the Great Learning, The Mind-Method of the Zuo Commentary on the Spring and Autumn, An Essay on the Influences of Laozi and Zhuangzi, An Explanation of the Daodejing, An Explanation of the Inner Chapters of Zhuangzi, On the Three Teachings, and The Finger-and-Palm of the Mystic Door. While he dwelt at Caoxi, the scholars who wore the scholar’s cap and bore their satchels came to ask the Way; of such was Feng Changli’s company, who in all cases brought their examination compositions to be corrected and passed. My teacher, with the diamond eye, pointed them out one by one from the tip of his brush. Of old, Zhang Zishao went to Jingshan and there solved the meaning of “investigating things” and “things being investigated.” Later, because he contested in the sutra-lecture hall, he was banished far to Hengpu, and standing there leaning on his book, his twin cross-legged feet were hidden. He once said that the karmic cases the elder of Jingshan brought up were like a thousand gates and ten thousand doors, all thrown open at one tread; it was no accident. My teacher’s compositions and preaching were not confined to the matter beneath the monk’s robe. Those who should be saved by the body of the great Da Luo immortal, to them he manifested the body of the great Da Luo immortal and preached the dharma; those who should be saved by the body of the great general, to them he manifested the body of the great general and preached the dharma; those who should be saved by the body of the scholar, the graduate, the minister, the king, to them he manifested the body of the scholar, the graduate, the minister, the king, and preached the dharma. Simply in this chronicle written at his death, the preaching is without bound, such as the patriarchs of old rarely beheld with their eyes. In my view, Confucius, wheeling round through the states, means the six perfections and the ten thousand practices--it is the Tathāgata’s Chan. The self-cultivation and full-realization of nature of Zengzi and Mencius, knowing Heaven and establishing the mandate--it is the patriarchs’ Chan. My teacher, making himself a Buddha and a patriarch, did not depart from Confucius and Mencius. And I, a little one who learn Confucius and Mencius, would I dare abandon the Buddha and the patriarchs? Buddha and patriarch, Confucius and Mencius: though their practice of transformation be each in a different quarter, how could their journey’s end be in a different place? Confucius and Mencius, when they take rebirth, must return to the Pure Land. And I, returning to the Buddha, will in nothing abandon the Confucian. In the eastern land and in the western quarter, in every place and every moment, I shall see Confucius and see the Buddha, and forever take refuge in the Immortal Ancestor. From this time on, for life after life, in fame, rank, riches, and honor I will not contend to be first among men; in reading books and learning the Way I will not fall behind. The four rules of the Doctrine of the Mean, I strive for them yet cannot; the three warnings of the Analects, I hope to learn them. Just now the Hu comes and the Han comes; the body is in the midst of the great dream, and I would have all under heaven and above heaven truly hear these words. A verse says: The Pure Land, mind alone--my heart longs for the west; the one thread of the Mount Ni, set upon coming east. East and west, coming and going, I rest upon Zeng and Mencius; whether I die young or live long, the body is cultivated in the undivided womb. Again: Thin soup and the three books are the true riches; the fish-trap and the rabbit-snare, nine turnings, win the spirit’s flight. The household’s immortals and the world’s Buddhas hold no separate thought; in the end, the scholar’s cap is the very giving over of the robe.

The dharma-master Suhua, of the Xu lineage, made a verse and a preface on the chronicle’s narrative and commentary, saying: In the summer of the jiaxu year I lodged at the Huanzhu Hermitage in Wu and saw Zhu Baimin’s annotated chronicle of Old Man Han, and regretted that his comments still held much of the Confucian scholar’s view and were not enough to know the state of a great man. In the bingzi year I fell ill and entered Mount Jiuhua, where all my hundred thoughts turned cold and my books were scattered, not one remaining. In the spring of the xinmao year, wandering in a dream to Changgan, I saw again the chronicle of Old Man Han as narrated and commented by Tan Saoyan, and it was able, over the whole course of the great affair, to verify the false and examine the true, and to set forth fully the spiritual power and the power of the Way. It had been gained during his eastern travels through direct oral instruction, face to face, and was the fruit of more than a morning or an evening. For when I think of the renxu year, when Zhixu first left home, I dreamed of Old Man Han three times; and in the winter of the guihai year, just as he was about to enter stillness, he showed me a dream again. All these were his compassionate and true aid--could they be accident? The people of the world, blinded to the oneness of waking and dream, recklessly take waking as real and dream as empty. Little do they know that the waking of this world is not real, and the dream that transcends the world is not empty. The Peaceful Practice chapter of the Lotus begins from the first rousing of the mind and ends in the all-knowing wisdom, never leaving one dream. The gate of Old Man Han’s awakening, gained in his life, came for the most part from dreams, and so his writings are also named “The Collected Wanderings of a Dream.” Yet were it not for the layman Tan, who could believe it? I respectfully offer a verse: Waking and dream are from the mind alone; the mind alone, how is it empty or real? The deluded hold both to be empty; the awakened hold both to be real. The living take dream as the response; the Buddha takes dream as the answer. Response and answer are one mind only, never to be fathomed. Since the Old Man’s dream is not empty, Zhixu’s dream too must be real. I do not tell this to the foolish; I permit only Saoyan to know.

In the winter-solstice month of the bingchen year of the Wanli reign, I went up with reverence to the Jizhao Hermitage on Mount Shuangjing, took refuge in my teacher Hanshan, and composed a verse of old to present. (At the time, Zhen was twenty-seven years of age, and went up Jingshan together with the dharma-master Xuanjin to invite him to open the hall at the Jingci of Hunan.)

I sigh that I am born late in the kalpa; the true dharma grows over with thorns. Monks and layfolk cross in confusion, teaching and school are judged by name and form. The chant of empty disputation opens, the shout and blow of the bare fist come forth. The monkey grasps the moon in the water,

The blind grieve at the sun in the sky. The moon in the water is a finger pointing; the sun in the sky, a white overhead. Long had I sought it in the midst of this, turning and turning, no trace to be found. Thought and deliberation are the household plots of ghosts;

The void still presses close. In the summer when the house falls, distinctly there is a thunderbolt. The matter of birth and death before my eyes, one word cannot turn it away. I beg of the clear-eyed man, to discuss what is so wondrous.

My master, the great dharma-king, wanders in the lion’s den. His flying staff shakes the sea-prison, his halberd leads the Yue and the Mo. The Pure Land is his home-town, Caoxi is his true blood-drop.

For many years the relic-pearl, in cremation saw the purple candle. The grotesqueries of the patriarch-court dissolve, the doubts and dizzying of the jewel-vehicle are released. South of the mountain, below the Wu gate, the dragons and elephants stand tall in ranks.
The golden tweezers vouchsafed to try, the hair-pearl is at hand. I wash my liver and bow to the twin feet, a karmic bond deep from long ago.
(The poems made in wandering the hills about the lake are all left unrecorded.)

In the late spring of the jiazi year of the Tianqi reign, lodging at the Shideng Hermitage in the capital of Yan, I learned by careful hearing of my teacher Hanshan’s news of stillness at Caoxi, and so gathered the monks and lay disciples and established a dharma-court for reciting the sutras and recollecting the Buddha. And so I composed the poem of distant grief, a long regulated verse of fifty-two rhymes, to mark my sorrow. (At the time, Zhen was in the capital taking the cultivation-exam as a Mingjing scholar, aged thirty-five, and had heard from afar the news that my teacher was showing stillness at Caoxi; tracing back to the tenth month of the guihai year, it was already near half a year past. In that year he passed the provincial examination.)

The master made the standard of gods and men; his spirit set forth in concentration and wisdom. His birth-star on the lofty brow was grave, the seal of the moon showed the white hair-ray. Transcending the ties, his thought was not of training; his nature’s affinity, the grace was self-auspicious. The Way being exhausted, the last leaves came;

Awakening to the great, he mended the falling net. The evil seed was driven to fork and gather, the pure emblems shook the bowl’s fragrance. In spring the great measure brimmed, in summer the fierce force spread. In the dragon’s wall, nine years of contemplation;

In the ice, he took part in the ten-thousand league direction. Answering the void, he drew to himself the wayfolk and the monks, proving the transformation and guiding the lords and kings. The sagely offering of the purple kṣāya, the merciful name sealed in the sovereign’s yellow. The savory provisions piled in abundance, the portrait of the crown-symbol was painted.

The great name is revered as the mountain and peak, the lofty rule shines upon the pillars and beams. The settled heir suffered the dharma-tribulation, repaying the state he took up the soldier’s rank. On the Yuetling the public road, at Caoxi the Sixth Patriarch’s field.

The secret cause spread over the miasmic air, the perfect guide pierced the barbarous wilds. The mad elephant lost its demonic power, the fierce dragon washed clean its poisoned bowels. Dwelling in obscurity his fame grew the greater, moving in peril his acts were the more good.

Giving precepts, monks and layfolk in throng; practicing charity, he aided swimmers and fliers. The dust of fragrance lingers in the chamber of meaning, the monkey’s fruit hangs on the Chan bed. The simple and the plain answered the Duke of Zhou and Confucius; the void and the bright cast the Old and Zhuang. In the lodging dawn he explored the translations;

The accumulated stones illumine the kept details. Feasting on the blossoms of heaven, he dispensed, and with the needle of healing he tended the assembly of jewels. His closing words, the worm that eats the wood; his general discourse, the sun that props Fusang. From his tongue came the bone of the dhāraṇī;

His breast opened the dark storehouse of the mysterious. The Lotus he urged with a beat of the hand, and doubt-verdicts he decided with the diamond. The Influences he spread as a hanging mirror, the Laṃkāvatāra unsealed its secret bag. He took up the brush and needed no craftsman; cross-legged, he completed whole chapters.

The Left Historian he glossed amid the Zhu and the Si; the arts of war he set by the Wei and the Yang. Knocking at the ford, the deep flavor poured out; unsealing the flute, the wise sound was prosperous. Wielding broom, without clinging wisdom, he chanted, and his verse had beneficence and health.

His argument had no obstruction even in one thing; the meeting of his meaning gathered by the side of the nine streams. The royal decree followed his flying staff, his full bearing was grand and strong. The dark banner rose above the Lu cliff, the dharma-standard descended the Heng and Xiang;

In the Yan market he repaid the vow of knowing, and in the prison he thought of the bones he treasured. The cremation verse of Shuangjing, the stele inscription of the village whose incense is of Brahma. In refuge and faith he entered the city of transformation, the karmic meeting of the Mirror-of-the-School hall. Looking up, the five purities,

The four norms of behavior good. The elders circled in sandalwood, the caps and girdles followed in long train. Lifting the child that clings in love, the lamp and grass he reasoned together. The pen recorded the eastern travels,

The heart’s vow was to stand in the snow. Hesitating, the cliff and the waterfall cut off, in a hush of deep years. The patient world was moved to the southern record, the wheel of compassion held the old territory. Baolin he followed and went, the Meiling he settled and left behind.

His appearance and passing shone in a different scene; the circle of mourning fell into a bitter frost. In nirvāṇa his hidden and manifest traces, in withered grief the white and the black were wounded. Turning back to the west his wheeled feet went, and Jambudvīpa lost the universal ferry.

The ritual officials demanded the posthumous canon, the regional commander guarded the soul’s array. The five-breasted goose-king fell still, the twin-forest deer-goddess died. In glory and mourning the heavenly rank was honored, his years and age-sufficient were ever revered.

The stūpa’s shadow holds the legacy of the teaching, the shrine’s soul flirts with the subtle light. The gate-disciples’ grief was the more intense, the hoped-for image rose in the dream. Far-reaching through ten thousand ages, I linger and shame at a single boat. If fortunate, one may diligently wipe and brush,
The remaining shade brings coolness.

(After this piece was finished, twenty-eight years passed before I saw the chronicle. What is in it of the old facts I gained all through direct oral instruction; and when I came to comment on the chronicle I knew it could be verified one by one.)

On the twentieth day of the third month in the gengyin year of the Shunzhi reign, lodging by chance to the left of Yuhua Terrace in Jiangning, I obtained the true record of the self-narrated chronicle of the Old Man Hanshan. I received it with reverence, read it with joy, bowed in homage, and praised it, obtaining ten quatrains. (At the time Zhen was sixty-one years old; the Way-friend Wang Jiyan, having for my sake found the complete chronicle at the east-chan monk’s quarters, sent it to my new lodging. Just then I was preparing to return to my boat and had moved it to the mouth of the river.)

The chronicle done, from the twin trees I look for the blossoming; the karmic bond of the Mirror-of-the-School was long a vain guess. After the ten-thousand li of Caoxi, amid the scattering of the turmoil, the flesh-Buddha of the Western Forest has at last returned.
Of the Wuru and Caoxi dharma-heirs many,
Ten generations of aged Chan folk of Moling. The golden needle’s crossing--where shall it be sought? Embroidered swans bathe in the brocade waves.
From the river a flying letter to the dharma-successor,
A word from heaven that confers the robe-pearl. The radiance of India and of the Zhu-and-Si spreads far; who says the world divides the Buddha from the Confucian?
Taking refuge at Shuangjing, the years pass over Wu; commonly he entered concentration and attended the twin feet.
I have heard in full the solemn affairs after his death; spreading the dharma, he forgot his body to gather the withered.
One shout, and he personally taught the Pure Land rebirth; one word, and again the spirits and demons were startled.
His face like the full moon, his lips like the crescent moon; the complete marks of his compassionate might cannot be painted.
Preaching the dharma, from the first he needed no device; ascending the hall, one saw only the Buddha’s dignified bearing. Setting aside the staff, his loving heart was great,
Leading the assembly home through mud and through heavenly flowers.
In that year I transcribed with my own hand the Eastern-Travel Collected; scroll after scroll of fragrant-light is a living topic. Unlike the men of the quarters who pick out phrases,
Who blur the heart and blurt it out, hawking their brilliance.
The Buddha-eye wholly free, the Confucian eye is reverenced; the flesh-body clearly shows the dharma-body remains. Over all under heaven and over all the earth the light spreads,
Covering the single transmission that points directly at the gate.
In those days Zibai’s heart and liver were the same; from far he sent the Kang-hymn to seal the seal of Master Han. The skull’s image appeared at Caoxi, and the light of Wu and Yue met in it.

Counting the years of Caoxi, just over a thousand have passed; across from Baolin the flesh-body is handed on. The five hundred of the Confucian gate who rose to famous lives, in doubled remembrance should know the karmic bonds of eons.

(Patriarch Lu was born in the spring of the wuxu year of the Zhenguan era of Tang; Patriarch Hanshan passed on in the winter of the guihai year of the Tianqi era of the present Ming; between them are one thousand and seventeen years.)

I journeyed by river to give a narrative and comment on my teacher Hanshan’s chronicle. In seven days I reached my home, in the Hall of Compositions; the work of commenting on the chronicle being finished, I sighed over it and obtained two quatrains.

Seven days of mind-fast, and I sat and forgot; the river-town hurriedly brought me to the He-town. At the water-window I faced the Baolin seat, and my mind wandered at the desk to the Mirror-of-the-School hall. (Self-answering.)

The karmic bonds of eons I remember and do not forget; a single drop of Caoxi is my home-town. I emptied my whole chest of the meaning that comes from the west, and only upon reaching the shore knew the Hall of Compositions.

On the first day of the intercalary second moon in the xinmao year of the Shunzhi reign, again lodging by chance to the left of Yuhua Terrace, I set the artisans at work to print my teacher Hanshan’s chronicle with narrative and comment; rejoicing at the intent, I praised myself and obtained four quatrains.

One generation honors the three Buddhist-fathers, three reigns fix the succession in a single cosmos. Gathering the state histories I gloss the Chan histories, and packing up the schools I seal the Buddhist gate. (Self-answering.)

Of withering and flourishing I speak not with the old masters; laughing and weeping, I write straight, another cosmos. The karmic meeting and the hour are truly strange: the mat of Confucius alone can requite the gate of the Buddha. (Second answering.)

Enmity and gratitude, the kalpa-ashes, are swallowed in the vast sea; right and wrong’s wheel and sun are given to the cosmos. The brush of the Spring and Autumn prunes the meaning that comes from the west; the mind-transmission of the Zuo is the undivided gate. (Third answering.)

The courts and the palaces pass through sun and moon; icebergs and the poisonous sea are traversed of the cosmos. The hidden meaning of the Plain King’s, the brush of the Empty King; the mind-mirror hangs the same, and there are those at the gate.

(By the three Buddhist-fathers are meant Patriarch Hanshan and the masters Daguan and Lian. By the three reigns are meant the temple-god shrine and the prince and the prince’s son. By the old masters are meant the ministers who in their day strove to establish the heir-apparent. By the withering and flourishing and right and wrong is meant the grudges and estrangements of the officials; the chronicle is the Chan history, the narrative is the state history.)

The old disciple who named the Mirror-of-the-School hall, Fu Zheng, the former scholar, holder of the office of the Southern Directorate of Education, of the sweep-history clan of the Man of Jing in the town of Zui, the layman of the One Way, Tan Zhenmo, looking south, bows in homage, with all five limbs upon the ground, and respectfully inscribes these few words at the end of the scroll.

The disciple Xiang Guifang of Jiahe, day and night clasped arms with the master in Shaoyang. When I was sent by commission to Kuangzhou, because my son died young, my heart was wounded and I fell ill, with scarce any sign of recovery; so I specially invited the master to visit me at Kuang and begged a method of liberation. When he arrived he showed me, saying: “People in the world, if anything crosses them in the least, the small ones rage at it, the great ones hate it. For a parent to raise a child--what loving tenderness! Yet suddenly to lay upon the body a vexation never known in a lifetime, and not to hate it greatly, is the friend who mourns to the point of despair. Amid this deep-autumn poisonous mist, looking back on my home a thousand li away, I would have you practice self-dispelling.” I, awe-struck, bowed and received the instruction, and was fortunate to recover unharmed; all this is my master’s pointing out order to my darkness, that I have come to this day. Before long the master fell ill; the medicines of the official boat carried him for half a year before he was healed, and the Nanhua case was settled. This all came from my colleagues joining their strength to uphold the public judgment, which the judicial intendant could not bend, and they put the responsible one to the law. The master then entered the mountain of Dinghu, and I saw him off at the Fu River, darkly parting. After more than ten years, when the master saw Daguan’s relic into the stūpa, he specially visited my thatched hut, and we sat knee to knee recounting old things, as though waking from a dream. Pity that at every step a thousand people thronged to bow, and so we hastily parted and he went. Now the master has already received the robe and bowl of the Sixth Patriarch; a single pool of water in Caoxi shines with the same light as sun and moon. But I am old, and cannot drag my feet eastward to bow in ranks before the Seventh Patriarch; I have only a thousand lines of a letter, hid in a stone box, which morning and evening I reverently honor, and steep myself in the fragrance of sandalwood to steady my last breath. And so, because the layman Tan Saoyan knows the true faith of the flesh-body’s chronicle, I respectfully praise.

Unfinished the old dharma-field of Nanhua; the general, understanding the words, revealed a ray of light. One couch at the Tiger Brook, cold as the fleeting clouds; the thousand characters of the Buddha-run, fragrant in the thatched room. The court-bestowed kṣāya beyond the embroidered dragon,
